analysis.one_liner: Lets federal safety regulators set design, testing, labeling, and recall rules for guns and ammunition like other consumer products.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in August 1994 with 7 cosponsors, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and then its crime subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated guns, gun parts, ammunition, and BB guns like other consumer products. It directed the Treasury Department to write safety regulations for how firearms are designed, made, and sold, to order recalls or refunds of dangerous models, to inspect manufacturers and dealers, and to keep a public clearinghouse of data on gun injuries and deaths. It also let private citizens sue for damages when a firearm product violated the rules, and it set civil fines and up to two years in prison for knowing violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to firearm injury and death: the bill aimed to keep products with unreasonable risks off the market through safety testing and certification, labeling so buyers know who made a gun, recalls and refunds for defective or dangerous products, public reporting of gun-injury data, and the right to sue violators for damages with possible attorney's fees [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to test firearm products and certify they meet federal safety regulations before sale, and to notify the government before making new types of firearm products [S2][S3].

Lets the Treasury Secretary order recall, repair, replacement, or refunds for a firearm product found to pose an unreasonable risk of injury or be defective, and to ban manufacture or sale of products that remain unreasonably risky [S2][S3].
Authorizes inspections of places where firearm products are made or stored, requires record-keeping open to inspection, and bans stockpiling ahead of new regulations taking effect [S2][S3].

Creates a Firearms Violence Information Clearinghouse, ongoing federal research into gun deaths and injuries, and annual public reporting, reversing the practical blackout on federal gun-safety data [S2][S3].

Gives injured people and other interested parties the right to sue for damages or to enforce the law in federal court, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs, and preserves all existing state-law remedies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers, including pawnbrokers, who would bear the cost of testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, inspections, potential recalls and refunds, civil fines per violation, and lawsuits [S2][S3]. Some of that cost would likely be passed to buyers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun and ammunition makers and dealers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on manufacturers and dealers, including small dealers and pawnbrokers, and would likely raise prices for buyers [S3].

The Secretary's discretion is broad: the power to prohibit manufacture, importation, or sale of any product deemed an unreasonable risk, plus the stockpiling ban, could sharply restrict the availability of firearms that lawful owners want to buy [S3].
Private enforcement by 'any interested person' invites litigation against dealers and manufacturers beyond actual injury cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's framework mirrors what consumers already get for cars, toys, and household products — safety standards, recalls, and public data — applied to a product that kills and injures tens of thousands of Americans a year. The trade-off is real: compliance costs, higher prices, and broad agency power over which guns may be made and sold. Honest supporters would have to acknowledge that 'unreasonable risk' determinations would rest heavily on one executive-branch official's judgment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Major Owens (D-NY) introduced the Firearms Safety and Violence Prevention Act on August 4, 1994 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on August 4, 1994, and to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice on August 9, 1994 [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995, and the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers are better off: they remained outside any consumer-product-style safety regulation, with no federal testing, labeling, recall, or record-inspection regime of the kind the bill would have imposed. Gun buyers who value price and availability over safety standards also avoided the bill's costs and restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers, unregulated as products

for.name: Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 7 of 258 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all seven cosponsors were Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee / Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: National Rifle Association and firearms industry
against.what_they_did: Fought expansion of federal regulation of firearms throughout the era; the bill received no committee action in the months after its introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded supporters are the Democratic sponsor and seven Democratic cosponsors, so the bill never revealed whether it had broader or cross-party backing [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have subjected guns, parts, ammunition, and even BB guns to safety standards, testing and certification, labeling, factory inspections, recalls, per-unit civil fines, and private lawsuits. Their gain from the bill dying was continued freedom from any consumer-product regulation of firearms.
Dealers would have faced labeling duties, record-keeping open to federal inspection, recall and refund obligations, and liability in private suits. They benefit from the bill's death.
